concerns.description: All experiments use 2012–2015 data with 5-fold cross-validation. Forward-testing on 2013, 2014, 2015 (Figure 2b) shows slightly worse performance than CV, but this discrepancy is not explained. Generalization to pre-2012 or post-2015 data is untested.

Test on pre-2012 data (if available) to assess backward generalization. Investigate why forward-testing underperforms CV. Release code and baseline implementations as supplementary materials. Conduct sensitivity analysis on baseline hyperparameters to ensure fair comparison. Report whether baselines were optimized on the same 2012–2015 dataset or on their original data periods.

concerns.title: Conceptual novelty is limited; primarily engineering and empirical validation
concerns.description: The paper adapts existing IR weighting schemes (Rekabsaz et al. 2016b) to sentiment analysis and applies standard fusion methods (stacking, MKL, early fusion). The core contribution is empirical validation on 10-K data rather than a new conceptual frame. The temporal drift and sector-specific findings are interesting but underdeveloped as theoretical insights.

For sector-specific findings, develop a theory of when domain-specific training helps vs. hurts (e.g., sample complexity thresholds). Reframe contributions as 'domain-specific insights' rather than 'methodological novelty'.

alternative_interpretations: Temporal drift (Figure 1a) may reflect market regime changes (2008 financial crisis, post-crisis recovery) rather than conceptual drift in report writing. The 2012–2015 cluster may be more predictive due to market stability, not report coherence.

Sector-agnostic control experiment (Figures 3a–3b) supports data scarcity hypothesis, but lexical ambiguity could be a secondary factor. If data were doubled, sector-specific improvements might emerge, but this is untested.

Text feature stability in long-term prediction (Figure 2a, Q5–Q8) could reflect that text captures current market conditions (which persist) rather than forward-looking risk. Alternative explanation: market-only features degrade because volatility is mean-reverting, while text features capture persistent risk factors.

Extended IR weighting (B̂M25) improvement over base schemes (BM25) could be due to regularization effect of similarity-weighted terms rather than genuine semantic insight. Simpler regularization (e.g., L2 penalty) might achieve similar results.

Stacking outperformance (Table 1) could be due to meta-learner learning non-linear combinations of base model outputs, which early fusion cannot capture. MKL underperformance may reflect mklaren approximation rather than fundamental limitation of kernel-based fusion.
Improvement margins (r² 0.439 vs. 0.395) may be inflated by overfitting to 2012–2015 data. Pre-2012 or post-2015 data could show smaller improvements, suggesting limited generalization.
transparency_notes: This review assesses novelty from a disruptive-thinking lens, which protects unconventional ideas from being penalized for divergence from mainstream literature. However, this paper is not unconventional—it applies established IR techniques to a known domain. The disruptive lens reveals that the paper lacks a fundamentally new conceptual frame.

The temporal drift finding (3–4 year cycles) is the most novel contribution, but it is underdeveloped. With statistical validation and mechanistic explanation, this could become a significant insight. Currently, it is observational.

The sector-specific finding (general models outperform sector-specific models) is counter-intuitive and valuable, but it reduces to a data scarcity argument. The paper does not develop a theory of when domain-specific training helps vs. hurts.
Statistical significance testing is absent throughout. This is a critical gap for a novelty assessment, as improvements without significance may not constitute genuine innovation.
The paper is well-executed empirically (comprehensive ablations, clear methodology, reproducible setup), but empirical validation of existing methods is not the same as conceptual novelty.
Improvements are modest (~10% relative gain) and may not justify the added complexity of extended IR weighting and stacking. Simpler baselines might achieve similar results.

The paper would be strengthened by: (1) statistical significance testing, (2) temporal drift mechanistic explanation, (3) sector-specific lexicon testing, (4) time-series cross-validation, (5) ablation studies on hyperparameters, (6) nested cross-validation for stacking.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The paper applies established IR weighting techniques (Rekabsaz et al. 2016b) to sentiment analysis and uses standard fusion methods (stacking, MKL). While the application to 10-K volatility prediction is novel, the methodological contribution is primarily engineering and empirical validation rather than conceptual innovation. The temporal drift finding is interesting but underdeveloped as a theoretical contribution.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If the temporal drift finding were validated statistically and explained mechanistically (e.g., showing that drift reflects market regime changes or linguistic evolution), it could constitute a novel contribution to understanding financial text dynamics.

If the paper developed a theory of domain adaptation (e.g., quantifying when sector-specific training helps vs. hurts as a function of sample size and feature complexity), the sector-specific findings could be elevated from empirical observations to theoretical insights.
If improvements were statistically significant (p < 0.05) and robust across multiple datasets and time periods, the modest empirical gains would be more credible as genuine innovations.

If the paper compared extended IR weighting with simpler regularization methods (e.g., L2-penalized lexicon expansion) and showed that IR weighting is fundamentally superior (not just a regularization artifact), the methodological contribution would be stronger.

If the paper conducted time-series cross-validation and showed that results generalize to pre-2012 and post-2015 data, temporal generalization concerns would be addressed and the contribution would be more robust.

The temporal drift and sector-specific findings are interesting observations but lack theoretical development. A disruptive contribution would introduce a new conceptual frame (e.g., a theory of how financial text evolves, or a principle for when domain-specific training helps). specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: This paper proposes word embedding-extended IR term weighting schemes (B̂M25, T̂C, T̂FIDF, T̂F) combined with stacking-based late fusion to predict stock volatility from 10-K Risk Factors sections. The core claim is that extending IR weighting via word embeddings significantly outperforms prior sentiment analysis methods (Kogan et al. 2009, Wang et al. 2013, Tsai & Wang 2014). Secondary claims address temporal drift in 10-K content (3–4 year cycles), sector-level performance variation, and the counter-intuitive finding that general models outperform sector-specific models due to data scarcity. As a claim verifier, I assess the evidence supporting these assertions against the manuscript text, prior work, and methodological soundness. The paper presents consistent empirical improvements (r² 0.439 vs. 0.395 for text-only; 0.527 vs. 0.484 for text+market) but lacks statistical significance testing, hyperparameter ablation, and temporal generalization beyond 2012–2015. The temporal drift analysis is visually apparent but not statistically validated. Sector-specific findings rest on two anecdotal lexical examples ('fire', 'beneficial') without systematic polysemy analysis. The stacking design introduces potential data leakage (70–30 split without nested cross-validation) and meta-learner overfitting risks. Overall, the evidence is suggestive but insufficient to robustly support the strength of the main claims without additional validation.
logical_argument_graph: Premise 1: IR term weighting extended via word embeddings (Eq. 3) captures sentiment more effectively than lexicon-only approaches (Tsai & Wang 2014).
Premise 2: Extended schemes (B̂M25, T̂C, etc.) show consistent improvements over base schemes in Table 1 (e.g., B̂M25 r²=0.439 vs. BM25 r²=0.433).
Premise 3: Stacking fusion (r²=0.527) outperforms early fusion (r²=0.473) and MKL (r²=0.488) in Table 1.
Premise 4: 10-K reports exhibit temporal drift in 3–4 year cycles (Figure 1a cosine similarity heatmap shows three clusters: 2006–2008, 2009–2011, 2012–2015).
Premise 5: Performance improves when dropping older years (Figure 1b: r² increases from ~0.25 to ~0.40 when using 2012–2015 only).
Premise 6: Sector-specific models underperform general models (Figures 3a–3b) despite sector-specific risk factors existing (lexical examples: 'fire' in energy, 'beneficial' in healthcare).
Premise 7: Sector-agnostic control (random sampling of same size) performs similarly to sector-specific, supporting data scarcity hypothesis.
Premise 8: Text+Market features maintain r²~0.35–0.40 across Q5–Q8, while Market baseline drops to ~0.15–0.20 (Figure 2a).
Conclusion 1: Word embedding-extended IR weighting significantly outperforms prior methods for volatility prediction.
Conclusion 2: Stacking fusion is superior to early fusion and MKL for combining text and market features.
Conclusion 3: Temporal drift in 10-K content justifies using 2012–2015 data; older data introduces noise.
Conclusion 4: General models generalize better than sector-specific models due to training data scarcity, not lack of sector-specific signals.
Conclusion 5: Text features provide more stable long-term volatility predictions than market-only baselines.
Critical Gap: No statistical significance testing (p-values, confidence intervals) undermines all comparative claims.
Critical Gap: Stacking design (70–30 split) risks data leakage and meta-learner overfitting without nested cross-validation.
Critical Gap: Temporal drift causality asserted but not tested; alternative explanations (market regime changes, lexicon evolution, data quality) not ruled out.
Critical Gap: Sector-specific findings based on two anecdotal examples; no systematic polysemy analysis or sector-specific lexicon testing.

identified_claims.claim_label: Word embedding-extended IR weighting outperforms prior methods
identified_claims.claim_text: Word embedding-extended IR term weighting schemes (B̂M25, T̂C, T̂FIDF, T̂F) significantly outperform prior state-of-the-art sentiment analysis methods for volatility prediction from 10-K reports
evidence: Table 2: Text-only r² 0.439 (our method) vs. 0.395 (Tsai 2014) vs. 0.345 (Wang 2013); MSE 0.132 vs. 0.142 vs. 0.154
Table 2: Text+Market r² 0.527 (our method) vs. 0.484 (Tsai 2014) vs. 0.499 (Wang 2013); MSE 0.111 vs. 0.122 vs. 0.118
Table 1: Extended schemes (B̂M25 r²=0.439, T̂C r²=0.427) outperform base schemes (BM25 r²=0.433, TC r²=0.425)
Methodology (4.1, Eq. 3): Extension mechanism via t̂cdi(t) = tcdi(t) + Σ sim(t,t′)tcdi(t′) with cosine similarity threshold 0.70
uncertainty_flags: No statistical significance testing: p-values, confidence intervals, or hypothesis tests absent. Improvements may be within noise (11% relative gain for text-only: 0.439 vs. 0.395).
Baseline reproducibility unclear: Wang et al. (2013) and Tsai & Wang (2014) reproduced but implementation details sparse; exact replication not verified.
Limited baseline coverage: Only three prior methods compared; broader baseline coverage (e.g., deep learning approaches, other IR schemes) absent.
Cross-validation on 2012–2015 subset only: Generalization to other temporal periods untested; temporal leakage risk (standard 5-fold CV on sequential data).
Improvement margins modest in some cases: Text+Market 0.527 vs. Tsai 2014 0.484 = 8.9% relative gain; statistical robustness unknown.

identified_claims.claim_label: Stacking fusion outperforms early fusion and MKL
identified_claims.claim_text: Stacking-based late fusion of textual and market features achieves superior performance compared to early fusion and MKL approaches
evidence: Table 1: Stacking r²=0.527 (MSE=0.111) vs. MKL r²=0.488 (MSE=0.126) vs. Early Fusion r²=0.473 (MSE=0.125)
Methodology (4.3, lines 425–440): Stacking described as 'computationally inexpensive' with 70–30 train–test split on training data
Results (line 545): MKL noted as having 'highest computational complexity' among fusion methods
uncertainty_flags: Data leakage risk: Stacking uses 70–30 split on training data without nested cross-validation; meta-learner may overfit to base model outputs.
Hyperparameter sensitivity: Stacking split ratio (70–30) not ablated; optimal ratio unknown. Meta-learner choice (SVM) not justified.
MKL implementation incomplete: Uses mklaren approximation; full MKL performance unknown. Approximation quality not assessed.
Computational efficiency claims unsubstantiated: 'Computationally inexpensive' stated but no runtime measurements, complexity analysis, or wall-clock time comparisons provided.
No statistical significance testing: Differences between fusion methods (0.527 vs. 0.488 vs. 0.473) not tested for significance.
Limited fusion method coverage: Only three fusion approaches tested; other late fusion methods (weighted averaging, Bayesian model averaging) not compared.

identified_claims.claim_label: 10-K reports exhibit 3–4 year temporal drift cycles
identified_claims.claim_text: 10-K report content exhibits temporal drift in 3–4 year cycles; reports from 2012–2015 form a coherent cluster more predictive than older data
evidence: Figure 1a: Cosine similarity heatmap shows three apparent clusters: 2006–2008, 2009–2011, 2012–2015 (high similarity within clusters, low between)
Figure 1b: r² improves from ~0.25 (2006–2015) to ~0.40 (2012–2015) when dropping older years sequentially
Dyer et al. (2016) cited as motivation: '10-K reports are getting more redundant and complex' (lines 101–110)
uncertainty_flags: Clustering validation absent: No statistical tests (silhouette score, Davies–Bouldin index, gap statistic) to validate cluster separation or optimal number of clusters.
Threshold for 'coherence' not specified: Cosine similarity heatmap visual but no quantitative threshold defining cluster boundaries.

Causality of drift unclear: Attributed to 'conceptual drift' (line 520) but alternative explanations not ruled out: (a) market regime changes (2008 financial crisis, post-crisis recovery), (b) lexicon evolution (Word2Vec trained on all reports, may reflect temporal shifts), (c) data quality changes (SEC filing standards, reporting practices), (d) sample composition changes (different companies, sectors over time).
Limited temporal span: Only 10-year window (2006–2015) examined; generalization to longer periods unknown. Cyclical pattern may not persist beyond 2015.
Confounding with data quality: Improvement in r² when dropping older years could reflect data quality issues rather than conceptual drift (e.g., OCR errors, incomplete digitization of older filings).
No analysis of drift mechanism: Which specific terms or topics drive the drift? Semantic shift analysis absent.

identified_claims.claim_label: General models outperform sector-specific models despite sector differences
identified_claims.claim_text: General models trained on all sectors outperform sector-specific models due to training data scarcity, though sector-specific risk factors and lexical ambiguities exist and become exploitable with larger datasets
evidence: Figures 3a–3b: General model bars consistently higher than sector-specific bars across all 11 sectors
Table 3: Sector sample sizes range from 115 (dur) to 847 (fin); general model trained on 3,892 reports
Sector-agnostic control (random sampling of same size as sector-specific) performs similarly to sector-specific, supporting data scarcity hypothesis

Lexical ambiguity examples: 'fire' in energy sector (explosion hazards) vs. other sectors (dismissal); 'beneficial' in healthcare/basic industries (beneficial owner, risk-related) vs. general positive sentiment (lines 775–799)
uncertainty_flags: Sector-agnostic control design flawed: Uses single random sample without cross-validation or multiple runs; sampling variance not quantified. Conclusion about data scarcity based on single experiment.

Threshold for 'sufficient data' not quantified: Paper claims sector-specific improvements would emerge 'with larger datasets' but provides no estimate of required sample size or data scaling analysis.
Lexical ambiguity analysis anecdotal: Only two examples ('fire', 'beneficial') provided; no systematic polysemy analysis across sectors. Frequency of ambiguous terms unknown.
Sector-specific lexicon not tested: Loughran & McDonald (2011) lexicon assumed unbiased across sectors; sector-specific lexicons not developed or evaluated. Potential lexicon bias not assessed.

Linear regression used for interpretability but not for final predictions: Sector-specific findings based on linear regression coefficients; generalization to SVM (used for final predictions) unclear.

Alternative explanations not ruled out: General model outperformance could reflect: (a) regularization effect of larger training set, (b) sector-agnostic features (e.g., market volatility, GARCH) dominating sector-specific text signals, (c) insufficient sector-specific signal in Risk Factors section.
No analysis of sector-specific performance variation: Why do some sectors (e.g., finance) show higher r² than others (e.g., energy)? Sector-specific characteristics not investigated.

identified_claims.claim_label: Text features provide more stable long-term volatility predictions
identified_claims.claim_text: Text-based features provide more stable long-term volatility predictions (beyond 1 year) compared to market-only baselines, which degrade rapidly
evidence: Figure 2a: Text+Market maintains r²~0.35–0.40 across Q5–Q8 (quarters 5–8, year 2), while Market baseline drops to ~0.15–0.20
Figure 2a: GARCH baseline also degrades rapidly in later quartiles (dashed line)
Text-only features show 'roughly similar performance between first four quartiles' (line 625), then slight degradation in Q5–Q8
uncertainty_flags: Degradation pattern may reflect market regime changes, not feature informativeness: Volatility clustering and mean reversion in financial markets could explain degradation of market-only baselines independent of text feature quality.

No out-of-sample temporal generalization: Figure 2b shows forward-testing (2013, 2014, 2015 test sets) slightly worse than cross-validation; discrepancy not explained. Generalization beyond 2015 untested.

Mechanism of text feature stability unexplained: Why do text features remain stable? Possible explanations: (a) information decay rate of text vs. market signals, (b) semantic persistence of risk disclosures, (c) text features capturing forward-looking risk while market features reflect current conditions. No analysis provided.
Confounding with feature fusion: Text+Market combines text and market features; improvement over Market baseline could reflect market feature contribution rather than text feature stability.
No analysis of which text features drive stability: Are all weighting schemes equally stable? Do extended schemes (B̂M25, T̂C) outperform base schemes in long-term prediction? Ablation absent.
Statistical significance of degradation not tested: Differences between Q1–Q4 and Q5–Q8 not tested for significance.

Alternative volatility measures not tested: Results specific to log standard deviation (Eq. 1); generalization to other volatility measures (realized range, GARCH conditional variance, tail risk) unknown.

This systematic approach enables identification of best-performing combinations and provides evidence for design choices.

Eq. 3: Word embedding extension mechanism with cosine similarity
Eq. 4–5: SVM regression formulation with kernel function
Eq. 6: MKL kernel combination criterion

concerns.title: Absence of statistical significance testing undermines all comparative claims
concerns.description: The paper reports point estimates (r², MSE) without confidence intervals, p-values, or hypothesis tests. Improvements over baselines (e.g., 0.439 vs. 0.395 = 11% relative gain) may reflect random variation rather than genuine superiority. This is a critical methodological flaw that affects the validity of all main claims (C1–C5).
evidence: Table 1–2: No confidence intervals, standard errors, or p-values reported
Results section (6.1–6.3): No statistical tests (t-tests, ANOVA, permutation tests) for comparing methods
Improvement margins: Text-only 0.439 vs. 0.395 (11% relative); Text+Market 0.527 vs. 0.484 (8.9% relative) without significance assessment
Cross-validation: 5-fold CV used but no reporting of fold-wise variance or confidence intervals
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Add statistical significance testing: (1) Report 95% confidence intervals for all r² and MSE values; (2) Perform paired t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests comparing methods on cross-validation folds; (3) Report p-values and effect sizes (Cohen's d or similar); (4) Conduct permutation tests to assess significance of improvements over baselines.

concerns.title: Stacking design introduces data leakage and meta-learner overfitting risks
concerns.description: The stacking approach uses a 70–30 split on training data to generate meta-learner inputs without nested cross-validation. This design risks: (1) data leakage if the 30% validation set is not properly isolated, (2) meta-learner overfitting to base model outputs, (3) optimistic performance estimates. The paper does not address these risks or validate generalization.
evidence: Methodology (4.3, lines 425–440): 'split the training set into two parts (70%-30% portions)' without nested cross-validation
No mention of holdout validation for meta-learner or nested cross-validation procedure
Figure 2b shows forward-testing performance slightly worse than cross-validation (gap not explained), suggesting potential overfitting
Stacking described as avoiding 'lack of training data' (line 428) but no analysis of meta-learner generalization
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Implement nested cross-validation: (1) Use outer CV loop for model evaluation; (2) Use inner CV loop for stacking split and meta-learner training; (3) Report performance on held-out test set separate from stacking training data; (4) Compare stacking with other late fusion approaches (weighted averaging, Bayesian model averaging) to assess whether complexity is justified; (5) Ablate stacking split ratio (70–30 vs. 80–20 vs. 60–40) to assess sensitivity.

concerns.title: Temporal drift causality asserted but not tested; alternative explanations not ruled out
concerns.description: The paper attributes temporal drift in 10-K content to 'conceptual drift' (line 520) but does not test this hypothesis or rule out alternative explanations: (1) market regime changes (2008 financial crisis, post-crisis recovery), (2) lexicon evolution (Word2Vec trained on all reports, may reflect temporal shifts), (3) data quality changes (SEC filing standards, OCR errors), (4) sample composition changes (different companies/sectors over time). The clustering analysis lacks statistical validation.
evidence: Figure 1a: Cosine similarity heatmap shows three clusters but no statistical validation (silhouette score, Davies–Bouldin index, gap statistic)
Line 520: Drift attributed to 'conceptual drift' without testing alternative hypotheses
No analysis of which terms/topics drive the drift; semantic shift analysis absent
Limited temporal span: Only 10-year window examined; cyclical pattern may not persist beyond 2015
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Validate temporal drift causality: (1) Perform statistical clustering validation (silhouette score, Davies–Bouldin index, gap statistic); (2) Test alternative clustering methods (k-means, hierarchical) to assess robustness; (3) Analyze semantic shift: identify which terms/topics change most across clusters; (4) Control for confounds: (a) market regime (compare drift to VIX, market returns), (b) lexicon evolution (compare Word2Vec embeddings across time periods), (c) data quality (assess OCR error rates, filing completeness); (5) Extend temporal analysis beyond 2015 to assess whether 3–4 year cycle persists.

concerns.title: Hyperparameter choices not ablated or justified
concerns.description: Critical hyperparameters are fixed without ablation or sensitivity analysis: (1) PCA dimensionality (400), (2) SVM parameters (C=1.0, ε=0.1), (3) word embedding similarity threshold (0.70), (4) stacking split ratio (70–30). The paper states these follow 'previous studies' but does not verify optimality for this dataset or assess sensitivity.
evidence: Methodology (4.1, lines 351–365): 'initial experiments show 400 dimension as the optimum' but no details on range tested or cross-validation procedure
Methodology (4.1, lines 365–390): SVM parameters C=1.0, ε=0.1 follow 'previous studies' (Kogan et al. 2009, Tsai & Wang 2014) without justification for this dataset
Methodology (4.1, line 351): Cosine similarity threshold 0.70 follows 'Rekabsaz et al. (2016a, 2017) recommendations' without ablation
Methodology (4.3, line 425): Stacking split 70–30 stated without justification or sensitivity analysis
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Perform comprehensive hyperparameter ablation: (1) PCA dimensionality: test range 50–1000 with cross-validation; report performance curve; (2) SVM parameters: grid search over C ∈ {0.1, 1.0, 10} and ε ∈ {0.01, 0.1, 0.5}; (3) Similarity threshold: ablate 0.60, 0.70, 0.80; (4) Stacking split: test 60–40, 70–30, 80–20; (5) Report sensitivity of main results to hyperparameter choices; (6) Use cross-validation for hyperparameter selection, not just 'initial experiments'.

concerns.title: Temporal leakage risk in cross-validation on sequential data
concerns.description: The paper uses standard 5-fold cross-validation on sequential 10-K reports (2012–2015) without time-series cross-validation. This design risks temporal leakage: training data from later periods may influence predictions on earlier periods, inflating performance estimates. The forward-testing results (Figure 2b) are slightly worse than cross-validation, suggesting potential leakage.
evidence: Experiment Setup (5, lines 501–520): '5-fold cross validation' used without time-series CV
Figure 2b: Forward-testing (2013, 2014, 2015 test sets) shows slightly worse performance than cross-validation; gap not explained
No discussion of temporal structure of data or potential leakage
Assumption A6 (shared analysis): 'temporal structure of data (sequential reports) does not require time-series cross-validation' is unvalidated
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Implement time-series cross-validation: (1) Use forward-chaining CV: train on 2012, test on 2013; train on 2012–2013, test on 2014; train on 2012–2014, test on 2015; (2) Compare time-series CV results with standard 5-fold CV to quantify leakage; (3) Report performance gap between standard CV and forward-testing; (4) If gap is substantial, revise main claims based on more conservative time-series CV estimates.

concerns.title: Sector-specific findings based on anecdotal examples without systematic analysis
concerns.description: The paper claims sector-specific lexical ambiguities exist (C4) but provides only two examples ('fire', 'beneficial') without systematic polysemy analysis. No sector-specific lexicons are developed or tested. The sector-agnostic control uses a single random sample without cross-validation, making the data scarcity conclusion tentative.

uncertainty_flags: Statistical significance: No p-values, confidence intervals, or hypothesis tests reported. Improvements (11% relative for text-only, 8.9% for text+market) may be within noise. High confidence in this uncertainty.

Temporal drift causality: Attributed to 'conceptual drift' but alternative explanations (market regime changes, lexicon evolution, data quality, sample composition) not ruled out. Clustering lacks statistical validation. Medium-high confidence.
Stacking generalization: 70–30 split without nested cross-validation risks data leakage and meta-learner overfitting. Forward-testing slightly worse than CV (gap unexplained). High confidence.
Hyperparameter sensitivity: PCA=400, SVM C/ε, similarity threshold 0.70, stacking split 70–30 not ablated. Optimal values may vary by dataset. High confidence.
Baseline reproducibility: Prior methods reproduced but implementation details sparse. Fair comparison unclear. Medium confidence.
Sector-specific findings: Based on two anecdotal examples; no systematic polysemy analysis. Sector-agnostic control uses single random sample without cross-validation. Medium confidence.
Temporal generalization: Results limited to 2012–2015; pre-2012 and post-2015 performance untested. Temporal drift cycle may not persist beyond 2015. High confidence.
Temporal leakage: Standard 5-fold CV on sequential data without time-series CV. Forward-testing slightly worse than CV. Medium-high confidence.
Alternative volatility measures: Results specific to log standard deviation; generalization to other risk metrics unknown. Low-medium confidence.
Outlier filtering: 3σ threshold not justified; impact on extreme event prediction unknown. Low confidence.
Computational efficiency: Claims unsubstantiated; no runtime measurements or complexity analysis. Low-medium confidence.
alternative_interpretations: Temporal drift may reflect market regime changes (2008 financial crisis, post-crisis recovery) rather than conceptual drift in 10-K content. The 2006–2008 cluster coincides with pre-crisis period; 2009–2011 with crisis/recovery; 2012–2015 with post-crisis stability. This alternative explanation is not ruled out.

Improvement in r² when dropping older years could reflect data quality issues (OCR errors, incomplete digitization, SEC filing standard changes) rather than conceptual drift. Older filings may have lower quality, introducing noise.

General models outperforming sector-specific models could reflect regularization effect of larger training set rather than data scarcity per se. Sector-agnostic control (random sampling) may not isolate data scarcity effect if sector-specific features are weak.

Text+Market outperforming Market baseline could reflect market feature contribution rather than text feature stability. Ablation analysis (text-only vs. text+market) shows text contributes, but relative importance unclear.
Stacking outperforming early fusion and MKL could reflect meta-learner overfitting to base model outputs rather than genuine fusion superiority. Nested cross-validation would test this.
Extended weighting schemes (B̂M25, T̂C) outperforming base schemes could reflect overfitting to 2012–2015 data rather than genuine improvement. Generalization to other periods untested.
Sector-specific lexical ambiguities ('fire', 'beneficial') may be rare and have minimal impact on predictions. Frequency analysis would clarify.
Forward-testing performance slightly worse than cross-validation could reflect temporal leakage in standard CV rather than genuine generalization gap. Time-series CV would clarify.
transparency_notes: This review prioritizes evidence-based assessment of claims against manuscript text and prior work. Uncertainty is explicitly flagged rather than suppressed.
The paper's main claims (C1–C5) rest on modest empirical improvements without statistical significance testing. This is a critical limitation that affects all conclusions.
The temporal drift finding (C3) is visually apparent but lacks statistical validation. The causality is asserted rather than tested. This is a significant gap.
The sector-specific findings (C4) are based on two anecdotal examples without systematic analysis. The data scarcity hypothesis is plausible but not rigorously tested.
The stacking design (C2) introduces potential data leakage and meta-learner overfitting risks that are not addressed. This is a methodological concern that affects the fusion comparison.
The paper's strengths include systematic empirical comparison, consistent improvements over baselines, and novel temporal analysis. These are genuine contributions despite the limitations.
The paper's weaknesses are primarily methodological (lack of significance testing, hyperparameter ablation, temporal leakage) rather than conceptual. The ideas are sound but execution is incomplete.

This review does not recommend accept/reject but flags specific issues for revision. The paper would benefit from: (1) statistical significance testing, (2) hyperparameter ablation, (3) time-series cross-validation, (4) nested cross-validation for stacking, (5) systematic sector-specific analysis, (6) temporal generalization beyond 2015.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The paper adapts existing IR weighting techniques (Rekabsaz et al. 2016b) to financial sentiment analysis and combines them with standard fusion methods (stacking, MKL). The application is novel in domain (10-K volatility prediction) but the methodological components are not new. The temporal drift discovery and sector-specific analysis are interesting but lack rigorous validation. The work is incremental rather than disruptive.

If temporal generalization is demonstrated on post-2015 data, the practical utility would be clearer.

confidence_interval.rationale: The paper presents consistent empirical improvements over prior work and novel temporal analysis, supporting a moderate-to-high confidence in the quality of the empirical work. However, critical methodological gaps (lack of statistical significance testing, hyperparameter ablation, temporal leakage, stacking data leakage) and limited temporal generalization (2012–2015 only) reduce confidence in the robustness and generalizability of the claims. The lower bound (0.45) reflects the possibility that improvements are not statistically significant and temporal drift causality is unclear. The upper bound (0.75) reflects the genuine empirical contributions and systematic evaluation. The midpoint (~0.60) represents moderate confidence: the work is competent and makes contributions, but methodological rigor is insufficient for strong claims.

consensus_findings: Word embedding-extended IR term weighting schemes (B̂M25, T̂C, T̂FIDF, T̂F) show consistent empirical improvements over prior methods (Kogan et al. 2009, Wang et al. 2013, Tsai & Wang 2014) in both text-only (r² 0.439 vs. 0.395, ~11% relative gain) and text+market (r² 0.527 vs. 0.484, ~9% relative gain) settings, though improvements are modest and lack statistical significance testing.

Stacking-based late fusion achieves higher r² (0.527) than early fusion (0.473) and MKL (0.488) on the same dataset, but the 70–30 train–test split design introduces potential data leakage and meta-learner overfitting risks without nested cross-validation.

10-K reports exhibit temporal clustering into three groups (2006–2008, 2009–2011, 2012–2015) based on cosine similarity heatmap (Figure 1a), and model performance improves when restricting to 2012–2015 data (r² ~0.40 vs. ~0.25 for full 2006–2015 dataset), but causality of drift (conceptual drift vs. market regime changes vs. data quality) is unclear and lacks statistical validation.

General models trained on all sectors consistently outperform sector-specific models (Figures 3a–3b), and sector-agnostic controls (random sampling of same size) perform similarly to sector-specific models, supporting the data scarcity hypothesis, though the control uses single random sampling without cross-validation.

Text+Market features maintain stable r² (~0.35–0.40) across Q5–Q8 (year 2 prediction), while Market-only baselines degrade to r² ~0.15–0.20, suggesting text features provide more stable long-term volatility signals, though degradation patterns may reflect market regime changes or volatility clustering rather than feature informativeness.

The paper provides comprehensive systematic ablation studies comparing eight weighting schemes and three fusion methods with clear mathematical formulations and reproducible experimental setup, supporting methodological transparency.

All five main claims (C1–C5) lack statistical significance testing (p-values, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests), making it difficult to assess whether improvements are statistically robust or within noise margins.

This is the highest-confidence uncertainty across all reviewers.

Temporal drift causality: All reviewers note that drift is attributed to 'conceptual drift' but alternative explanations (market regime changes, lexicon evolution, data quality, sample composition) are not ruled out. Clustering lacks statistical validation (silhouette scores, Davies–Bouldin indices). This is a high-confidence uncertainty.

Stacking meta-learner generalization: All reviewers flag the 70–30 train–test split design without nested cross-validation as introducing potential data leakage and meta-learner overfitting. Forward-testing (Figure 2b) shows slightly worse performance than cross-validation, but the gap is not explained. This is a high-confidence uncertainty.

Hyperparameter sensitivity: All reviewers note that PCA dimensionality (400), SVM parameters (C=1.0, ε=0.1), similarity threshold (0.70), and stacking split ratio (70–30) are fixed without ablation studies. Optimal values may vary by dataset or weighting scheme. This is a high-confidence uncertainty.

Temporal generalization: All reviewers note that results are limited to 2012–2015 data. Generalization to pre-2012 or post-2015 periods is untested. Forward-testing on 2013–2015 shows slightly worse performance than cross-validation, suggesting potential overfitting or distribution shift. This is a high-confidence uncertainty.

Sector-specific lexical ambiguity: All reviewers note that sector-specific findings rest on two anecdotal examples ('fire', 'beneficial') without systematic polysemy analysis. Sector-agnostic control uses single random sampling without cross-validation. This is a medium-high confidence uncertainty.

Baseline reproducibility: Reviewers 2, 3, and 5 flag that prior methods are reproduced but implementation details are sparse. Exact replication is unclear, raising questions about fair comparison. This is a medium confidence uncertainty.

Temporal leakage in cross-validation: Reviewers 2, 4, and 5 note that standard 5-fold cross-validation on sequential data (10-K reports) may overestimate performance due to temporal leakage. Time-series cross-validation is not used. This is a medium-high confidence uncertainty.

Outlier filtering justification: Reviewers 2, 3, and 5 note that the 3σ threshold for volatility filtering is not justified, and impact on extreme event prediction is unknown. This is a low-medium confidence uncertainty.

Computational efficiency claims: Reviewers 2 and 5 note that claims about stacking being 'computationally inexpensive' and MKL having 'highest computational complexity' lack empirical support (no runtime measurements or complexity analysis). This is a low-medium confidence uncertainty.
model_diversity_effects: Structure_analyst (Reviewer 1) prioritizes logical coherence and identifies unvalidated assumptions, leading to a focus on the argument chain's internal consistency rather than empirical validation. This lens reveals that the paper's reasoning is coherent but rests on assumptions that are not independently tested.

Methodology_auditor (Reviewer 2) prioritizes statistical rigor and reproducibility, leading to identification of critical methodological gaps (no significance testing, hyperparameter ablation, temporal leakage, stacking design issues). This lens reveals that empirical validation is incomplete.

Novelty_assessor_incremental (Reviewer 3) treats the contribution as an evolutionary advance, focusing on consistent empirical improvements and systematic ablation studies. This lens leads to a more favorable assessment of the paper's contributions despite methodological gaps.

Novelty_assessor_disruptive (Reviewer 4) prioritizes conceptual innovation and theoretical development, leading to a critical assessment that the paper lacks a fundamentally new conceptual frame. The diversity of cognitive roles reveals that the paper's assessment depends critically on the evaluation framework: (1) logical coherence (Reviewer 1) vs. statistical rigor (Reviewer 2), (2) incremental novelty (Reviewer 3) vs. disruptive novelty (Reviewer 4), (3) evidence-based verification (Reviewer 5). Different frameworks lead to different conclusions about the paper's quality and contribution.

The model diversity also reveals that the paper's main weakness (lack of statistical significance testing) is consistently flagged across all cognitive roles, suggesting this is a robust finding rather than an artifact of a particular evaluation framework.

meta_review.editor_guidance: This paper presents a competent empirical study applying word embedding-extended IR term weighting to financial volatility prediction from 10-K reports. The work demonstrates consistent improvements over prior methods (11% relative gain for text-only, 8.9% for text+market) and provides novel temporal analysis revealing 3–4 year content cycles in 10-K reports. However, the paper has critical methodological gaps that must be addressed before publication: (1) Absence of statistical significance testing undermines all comparative claims; improvements may be within noise. (2) Stacking design (70–30 split) risks data leakage and meta-learner overfitting without nested cross-validation. (3) Temporal drift causality is asserted rather than tested; alternative explanations (market regime changes, lexicon evolution, data quality) are not ruled out. (4) Hyperparameter choices (PCA=400, SVM C/ε, similarity threshold, stacking split) are not ablated; sensitivity is unknown. (5) Temporal generalization is limited to 2012–2015; pre-2012 and post-2015 performance is untested. (6) Sector-specific findings rest on two anecdotal examples without systematic polysemy analysis. (7) Baseline reproducibility is unclear; implementation details are sparse. The paper would be significantly strengthened by: (1) Conducting paired t-tests or bootstrap confidence intervals on cross-validation folds; reporting p-values and effect sizes. (2) Implementing nested cross-validation for stacking; comparing with other late fusion approaches. (3) Validating temporal drift with statistical tests (silhouette scores, Davies–Bouldin indices); testing alternative clustering methods; investigating causality. (4) Providing ablation studies on PCA dimensionality, SVM hyperparameters, similarity threshold, and stacking split ratio. (5) Implementing time-series cross-validation to assess temporal leakage. (6) Conducting systematic polysemy analysis; testing sector-specific lexicons. (7) Providing detailed baseline implementation descriptions; releasing code for reproducibility. (8) Testing generalization on pre-2012 and post-2015 data if available. The paper makes genuine contributions (systematic empirical comparison, temporal drift discovery, sector-level analysis) but requires substantial methodological improvements to support the strength of its claims. Consider desk rejection if authors cannot address statistical significance testing and temporal leakage concerns; otherwise, request major revisions addressing the above issues.
meta_review.author_guidance: Your paper makes solid empirical contributions to financial volatility prediction, with consistent improvements over prior work and novel temporal analysis. However, reviewers have identified critical methodological gaps that must be addressed for publication. Here are the key issues and recommendations: (1) Statistical Significance Testing (CRITICAL): Add p-values, confidence intervals, and hypothesis tests for all comparative claims. Use paired t-tests or permutation tests on cross-validation folds. Report effect sizes (Cohen's d). Without significance testing, it is unclear whether your 11% improvement is robust or within noise. (2) Stacking Design (CRITICAL): Implement nested cross-validation to validate meta-learner generalization. Alternatively, use a three-way split (train base models, train meta-learner, evaluate on held-out test). Explain the forward-testing gap (Figure 2b). (3) Temporal Drift Analysis (MAJOR): Validate clustering with statistical tests (silhouette score, Davies–Bouldin index). Test alternative clustering methods (k-means, hierarchical). Investigate causality: rule out market regime changes, lexicon evolution, and data quality issues. Extend analysis beyond 2015 if possible. (4) Hyperparameter Ablation (MAJOR): Provide ablation studies on PCA dimensionality (50–1000), SVM C (0.1–10), ε (0.01–0.5), similarity threshold (0.6–0.8), and stacking split ratio (60–40, 70–30, 80–20). Report sensitivity of results. (5) Temporal Generalization (MAJOR): Implement time-series cross-validation (forward-chaining) to assess temporal leakage. Test on pre-2012 and post-2015 data if available. Explain why forward-testing underperforms cross-validation. (6) Sector-Specific Analysis (MODERATE): Conduct systematic polysemy analysis; identify all ambiguous terms. Test sector-specific lexicons. Repeat sector-agnostic control with multiple random seeds and cross-validation. (7) Baseline Reproducibility (MODERATE): Provide detailed implementation descriptions for all baselines. Report hyperparameters used. Release code and baseline implementations. (8) Computational Efficiency (MINOR): Provide runtime measurements and complexity analysis for fusion methods. Justify claims about stacking being 'inexpensive' and MKL being 'complex'. These revisions will significantly strengthen your paper and address reviewer concerns. The core ideas are sound; the execution requires additional rigor.
transparency_report: Five specialist reviewers with different cognitive roles (structure_analyst, methodology_auditor, novelty_assessor_incremental, novelty_assessor_disruptive, claim_verifier) were asked to assess the paper independently. Their analyses are synthesized below.

All reviewers agree that the paper presents consistent empirical improvements over prior work (11% relative gain for text-only, 8.9% for text+market) and provides novel temporal analysis of 10-K content drift. This consensus reflects genuine empirical contributions.

All reviewers flag the absence of statistical significance testing as a critical gap. This is the highest-confidence finding across all cognitive roles, suggesting it is a robust methodological concern rather than an artifact of a particular evaluation framework.

Reviewers disagree on the severity of methodological gaps: Reviewer 2 (methodology_auditor) treats them as major flaws undermining the paper's claims; Reviewer 3 (novelty_assessor_incremental) acknowledges them but frames them as limitations of modest improvements; Reviewer 4 (novelty_assessor_disruptive) treats them as evidence of limited innovation. The disagreement reflects different evaluation frameworks rather than factual disagreement.

Reviewers 1, 2, and 5 (structure_analyst, methodology_auditor, claim_verifier) provide detailed evidence-based assessments of specific claims (C1–C5) with explicit uncertainty flags. Reviewers 3 and 4 (novelty_assessors) focus more on the novelty and conceptual contribution of the work.

The shared extraction stage identified 12 assumptions (A1–A12) with varying risk levels. Reviewers prioritize different assumptions: Reviewer 2 emphasizes A6 (temporal leakage in cross-validation) and A8 (stacking data leakage); Reviewer 5 emphasizes A1 (volatility definition) and A3 (lexicon bias). This reflects different evaluation priorities.

Reviewers acknowledge that the paper's strengths (systematic ablation, consistent improvements, temporal analysis, sector insights) are genuine contributions. The disagreement is about how to weigh these contributions against methodological gaps.

The chaining notes from the shared extraction stage are reflected in reviewer assessments: Reviewer 2 (methodology_auditor) prioritizes ablation studies and statistical validation; Reviewer 5 (claim_verifier) prioritizes evidence-based assessment of claims. This suggests the shared extraction stage effectively identified key evaluation dimensions.

No reviewer recommends outright rejection, but all recommend substantial revisions addressing statistical significance testing, hyperparameter ablation, temporal leakage, and temporal generalization. This suggests the paper is borderline and could be acceptable with major revisions.

The confidence intervals reported by reviewers range from 0.35–0.75 (Reviewer 4) to 0.55–0.75 (Reviewer 1) to 0.45–0.65 (Reviewer 2) to 0.55–0.75 (Reviewer 3) to 0.45–0.75 (Reviewer 5). The midpoints cluster around 0.55–0.65, suggesting moderate confidence in the paper's quality with significant uncertainty about robustness and generalization.
epistemic_limits: Statistical Significance: The paper lacks p-values, confidence intervals, and hypothesis tests. Without statistical validation, it is impossible to assess whether improvements (11% relative gain) are statistically robust or within noise margins. This is a critical epistemic limit that affects the validity of all comparative claims.

Temporal Generalization: Results are limited to 2012–2015 data. Generalization to pre-2012 or post-2015 periods is unknown. The temporal drift finding is based on a single 10-year window; cyclical patterns may not persist beyond 2015. This limits the generalizability of the temporal drift hypothesis.

Causality of Temporal Drift: The paper attributes drift to 'conceptual drift' but does not test this hypothesis or rule out alternative explanations (market regime changes, lexicon evolution, data quality, sample composition). The clustering analysis lacks statistical validation. This limits causal inference about the source of temporal drift.

Hyperparameter Sensitivity: PCA dimensionality (400), SVM parameters (C=1.0, ε=0.1), similarity threshold (0.70), and stacking split ratio (70–30) are fixed without ablation. Optimal values may vary by dataset, weighting scheme, or prediction horizon. This limits understanding of the robustness of the approach.

Stacking Meta-learner Generalization: The 70–30 train–test split design without nested cross-validation introduces potential data leakage and meta-learner overfitting. Forward-testing (Figure 2b) shows slightly worse performance than cross-validation, but the gap is not explained. This limits confidence in the stacking fusion results.

Temporal Leakage in Cross-Validation: Standard 5-fold cross-validation on sequential data (10-K reports) may overestimate performance due to temporal leakage. Time-series cross-validation is not used. This limits the reliability of cross-validation estimates.

Baseline Reproducibility: Prior methods are reproduced but implementation details are sparse. Exact replication is unclear, raising questions about fair comparison. Differences in preprocessing, feature engineering, or hyperparameters could affect baseline performance. This limits confidence in the comparative claims.

Sector-Specific Lexical Ambiguity: Sector-specific findings rest on two anecdotal examples ('fire', 'beneficial') without systematic polysemy analysis. Frequency of ambiguous terms and their impact on predictions are unknown. This limits the generalizability of sector-specific insights.

Sector-Agnostic Control Design: The sector-agnostic control uses single random sampling without cross-validation or multiple runs. Sampling variance is not quantified. This limits confidence in the data scarcity hypothesis.

Alternative Volatility Measures: Results are specific to log standard deviation (Eq. 1). Generalization to other volatility measures (realized range, GARCH conditional variance, tail risk, downside volatility) is unknown. This limits the applicability of the findings to other risk metrics.
Outlier Filtering: The 3σ threshold for volatility filtering is not justified. Impact on extreme event prediction is unknown. This limits the applicability of the approach to tail risk prediction.

Computational Efficiency: Claims about stacking being 'computationally inexpensive' and MKL having 'highest computational complexity' lack empirical support. No runtime measurements or complexity analysis provided. This limits understanding of the practical trade-offs between fusion methods.

Long-term Prediction Mechanism: The paper does not explain why text features remain stable in long-term prediction (Q5–Q8). Degradation of market-only baselines may reflect market regime changes or volatility clustering rather than text feature informativeness. This limits understanding of the mechanism underlying long-term stability.

Generalization to Other Domains: The approach is evaluated only on 10-K reports for volatility prediction. Generalization to other financial documents (earnings calls, news, analyst reports), other markets (international), or other prediction tasks (price movements, earnings surprises) is unknown. This limits the scope of the contribution.

The paper provides systematic ablation studies comparing eight weighting schemes and three fusion methods with clear mathematical formulations and reproducible experimental setup. However, critical methodological gaps undermine confidence in the robustness of claims: (1) No statistical significance testing (p-values, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests) reported; improvements may be within noise. (2) Stacking design (70–30 train–test split) risks data leakage and meta-learner overfitting without nested cross-validation. (3) Temporal drift causality is asserted rather than tested; alternative explanations (market regime changes, lexicon evolution, data quality) not ruled out. (4) Hyperparameter choices (PCA=400, SVM C/ε, similarity threshold, stacking split) not ablated; sensitivity unknown. strengths: Systematic empirical comparison of eight weighting schemes and three fusion methods with consistent evaluation metrics (r², MSE) across multiple prediction horizons (8 quarters), enabling identification of best-performing combinations and providing evidence for design choices.

Consistent empirical improvements over three prior baselines (Kogan et al. 2009, Wang et al. 2013, Tsai & Wang 2014) in both r² and MSE metrics for both text-only and text+market configurations, demonstrated on the same dataset enabling fair comparison.

Novel temporal analysis revealing 3–4 year content cycles in 10-K reports (Figure 1a cosine similarity heatmap shows three distinct clusters: 2006–2008, 2009–2011, 2012–2015) with practical implications for model training and data collection.

Interpretable sector-level analysis with concrete lexical examples ('fire' in energy vs. other sectors, 'beneficial' in healthcare vs. general usage) demonstrating domain-specific understanding and providing actionable insights.

Counter-intuitive finding that general models outperform sector-specific models despite sector-level differences in risk factors, supported by sector-agnostic control experiment (Figures 3a–3b), challenging domain-adaptation intuitions.

Long-term prediction stability finding: text+market features maintain r² ~0.35–0.40 across Q5–Q8 (year 2 prediction) while market-only baselines degrade to r² ~0.15–0.20, suggesting text features capture forward-looking risk information.

Comprehensive dataset (3,892 reports from 1,323 companies across 10 years) with detailed preprocessing descriptions and promise to make data available, supporting reproducibility.
limitations: Absence of statistical significance testing (p-values, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests) undermines all comparative claims. Improvements are modest (11% relative for text-only: 0.439 vs. 0.395; 8.9% for text+market: 0.527 vs. 0.484) and may reflect random variation rather than genuine superiority. This is a critical methodological flaw affecting the validity of claims C1–C5.

Stacking design (70–30 train–test split on training data) introduces potential data leakage and meta-learner overfitting risks without nested cross-validation. Forward-testing (Figure 2b) shows slightly worse performance than cross-validation, but the gap is not explained. No nested cross-validation or holdout validation of meta-learner reported.

Temporal drift causality is asserted rather than tested. The paper attributes drift to 'conceptual drift' but does not rule out alternative explanations: (a) market regime changes (2008 financial crisis, post-crisis recovery), (b) lexicon evolution (Word2Vec trained on all reports), (c) data quality changes (SEC filing standards, OCR errors), (d) sample composition changes (different companies/sectors over time). Clustering lacks statistical validation (no silhouette scores, Davies–Bouldin indices, or alternative clustering methods tested).

Hyperparameter choices (PCA dimensionality=400, SVM C=1.0, ε=0.1, cosine similarity threshold=0.70, stacking split=70–30) are fixed without ablation studies or sensitivity analysis. The paper states these follow 'initial experiments' or 'previous studies' but provides no details on ranges tested or cross-validation procedures. Optimal values may vary by weighting scheme, dataset, or prediction horizon.

Temporal generalization is limited to 2012–2015 data. Generalization to pre-2012 or post-2015 periods is untested. Standard 5-fold cross-validation on sequential data (10-K reports) may overestimate performance due to temporal leakage; time-series cross-validation is not used. open_questions: Are the empirical improvements statistically significant? The paper reports r² 0.439 vs. 0.395 (11% relative gain) for text-only and r² 0.527 vs. 0.484 (8.9% relative gain) for text+market, but without p-values, confidence intervals, or hypothesis tests, it is unclear whether improvements are robust or within noise margins. What are the 95% confidence intervals for all reported r² and MSE values? Do paired t-tests on cross-validation folds show statistical significance (p < 0.05)?

What is the true generalization performance of the stacking meta-learner? The 70–30 train–test split design without nested cross-validation risks meta-learner overfitting to base model outputs. How does nested cross-validation performance compare with reported results? What is the meta-learner generalization error on a held-out validation set separate from stacking training data?

What is the causal mechanism underlying temporal drift in 10-K reports? The paper attributes drift to 'conceptual drift' but does not test this hypothesis. Is the drift due to (a) conceptual changes in report writing, (b) market regime changes (2008 financial crisis, post-crisis recovery), (c) lexicon evolution (Word2Vec embeddings change over time), (d) data quality changes (SEC filing standards, OCR errors), or (e) sample composition changes (different companies/sectors over time)? How do alternative clustering methods (k-means, hierarchical) compare with centroid-based clustering?

How sensitive are the results to hyperparameter choices? The paper fixes PCA dimensionality (400), SVM parameters (C=1.0, ε=0.1), similarity threshold (0.70), and stacking split ratio (70–30) without ablation. What are the performance curves for PCA dimensionality (50–1000), SVM C (0.1–10), ε (0.01–0.5), similarity threshold (0.6–0.8), and stacking split ratio (60–40, 70–30, 80–20)? Do optimal values vary by weighting scheme or prediction horizon?

Does temporal leakage inflate cross-validation estimates? Standard 5-fold cross-validation on sequential data (10-K reports) may overestimate performance. How does time-series cross-validation (forward-chaining) performance compare with standard 5-fold CV? Why does forward-testing (Figure 2b) show slightly worse performance than cross-validation? Is this due to temporal leakage, overfitting, or distribution shift?

All reviewers agree that the paper demonstrates consistent empirical improvements over prior work and provides novel temporal analysis. This consensus reflects genuine empirical contributions.

All reviewers flag the absence of statistical significance testing as a critical gap. This is the highest-confidence finding across all cognitive roles, suggesting it is a robust methodological concern rather than an artifact of a particular evaluation framework.

Reviewers disagree on the severity of methodological gaps: Reviewer 2 (methodology_auditor) treats them as major flaws undermining the paper's claims; Reviewer 3 (novelty_assessor_incremental) acknowledges them but frames them as limitations of modest improvements; Reviewer 4 (novelty_assessor_disruptive) treats them as evidence of limited innovation. The disagreement reflects different evaluation frameworks rather than factual disagreement.

The shared extraction stage identified 12 assumptions (A1–A12) with varying risk levels. Reviewers prioritize different assumptions based on their cognitive roles: Reviewer 2 emphasizes A6 (temporal leakage) and A8 (stacking data leakage); Reviewer 5 emphasizes A1 (volatility definition) and A3 (lexicon bias).

No reviewer recommends outright rejection, but all recommend substantial revisions addressing statistical significance testing, hyperparameter ablation, temporal leakage, and temporal generalization. This suggests the paper is borderline and could be acceptable with major revisions.

The confidence intervals reported by reviewers range from 0.35–0.75 (Reviewer 4) to 0.55–0.75 (Reviewer 1) to 0.45–0.65 (Reviewer 2) to 0.55–0.75 (Reviewer 3) to 0.45–0.75 (Reviewer 5). human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: This paper presents a competent empirical study applying word embedding-extended IR term weighting to financial volatility prediction from 10-K reports. The work demonstrates consistent improvements over prior methods (11% relative gain for text-only, 8.9% for text+market) and provides novel temporal analysis revealing 3–4 year content cycles in 10-K reports. However, the paper has critical methodological gaps that must be addressed before publication: (1) Absence of statistical significance testing undermines all comparative claims; improvements may be within noise. (2) Stacking design (70–30 split) risks data leakage and meta-learner overfitting without nested cross-validation. (3) Temporal drift causality is asserted rather than tested; alternative explanations (market regime changes, lexicon evolution, data quality) are not ruled out. (4) Hyperparameter choices (PCA=400, SVM C/ε, similarity threshold, stacking split) are not ablated; sensitivity is unknown. (5) Temporal generalization is limited to 2012–2015; pre-2012 and post-2015 performance is untested. (6) Sector-specific findings rest on two anecdotal examples without systematic polysemy analysis. (7) Baseline reproducibility is unclear; implementation details are sparse. RECOMMENDATION: Request major revisions addressing the above issues. The paper would be significantly strengthened by: (1) Conducting paired t-tests or bootstrap confidence intervals on cross-validation folds; reporting p-values and effect sizes. (2) Implementing nested cross-validation for stacking; comparing with other late fusion approaches. (3) Validating temporal drift with statistical tests (silhouette scores, Davies–Bouldin indices); testing alternative clustering methods; investigating causality. (4) Providing ablation studies on PCA dimensionality, SVM hyperparameters, similarity threshold, and stacking split ratio. (5) Implementing time-series cross-validation to assess temporal leakage. (6) Conducting systematic polysemy analysis; testing sector-specific lexicons. (7) Providing detailed baseline implementation descriptions; releasing code for reproducibility. (8) Testing generalization on pre-2012 and post-2015 data if available. The paper makes genuine contributions (systematic empirical comparison, temporal drift discovery, sector-level analysis) but requires substantial methodological improvements to support the strength of its claims. Consider desk rejection if authors cannot address statistical significance testing and temporal leakage concerns; otherwise, request major revisions addressing the above issues.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: Your paper makes solid empirical contributions to financial volatility prediction, with consistent improvements over prior work and novel temporal analysis. However, reviewers have identified critical methodological gaps that must be addressed for publication. Here are the key issues and recommendations: (1) STATISTICAL SIGNIFICANCE TESTING (CRITICAL): Add p-values, confidence intervals, and hypothesis tests for all comparative claims. Use paired t-tests or permutation tests on cross-validation folds. Report effect sizes (Cohen's d). Without significance testing, it is unclear whether your 11% improvement is robust or within noise. (2) STACKING DESIGN (CRITICAL): Implement nested cross-validation to validate meta-learner generalization. Alternatively, use a three-way split (train base models, train meta-learner, evaluate on held-out test). Explain the forward-testing gap (Figure 2b). (3) TEMPORAL DRIFT ANALYSIS (MAJOR): Validate clustering with statistical tests (silhouette score, Davies–Bouldin index). Test alternative clustering methods (k-means, hierarchical). Investigate causality: rule out market regime changes, lexicon evolution, and data quality issues. Extend analysis beyond 2015 if possible. (4) HYPERPARAMETER ABLATION (MAJOR): Provide ablation studies on PCA dimensionality (50–1000), SVM C (0.1–10), ε (0.01–0.5), similarity threshold (0.6–0.8), and stacking split ratio (60–40, 70–30, 80–20). Report sensitivity of results. (5) TEMPORAL GENERALIZATION (MAJOR): Implement time-series cross-validation (forward-chaining) to assess temporal leakage. Test on pre-2012 and post-2015 data if available. Explain why forward-testing underperforms cross-validation. (6) SECTOR-SPECIFIC ANALYSIS (MODERATE): Conduct systematic polysemy analysis; identify all ambiguous terms. Test sector-specific lexicons. Repeat sector-agnostic control with multiple random seeds and cross-validation. (7) BASELINE REPRODUCIBILITY (MODERATE): Provide detailed implementation descriptions for all baselines. Report hyperparameters used. Release code and baseline implementations. (8) COMPUTATIONAL EFFICIENCY (MINOR): Provide runtime measurements and complexity analysis for fusion methods. Justify claims about stacking being 'inexpensive' and MKL being 'complex'. These revisions will significantly strengthen your paper and address reviewer concerns. The core ideas are sound; the execution requires additional rigor.

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

top_documents.title: Document 2
top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

top_documents.title: Document 3
top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 🆕 4. Check for common problems in NLP papers
Codes: M1, G2
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor
Content: As a counter to common problems with reviews, there are also common problems with NLP papers. We do ask you to watch out for these and point them out when you see them. Above all else, published research should at least be technically sound and appropriately scoped. As with the above reviewer issues, it’s a case-by-case evaluation: some things in the list below may be appropriate in a given context, given that they are sufficiently motivated. We provide codes for different types of issues (e.g. M1, G2…) that can be referenced in discussions.

Content: n doubt, consider the scope described in ARR CFP and any relevant conferences (e.g. for October 2024 cycle the NAACL CFP specifies the special theme “NLP in a Multicultural World”. Hallucinated references or citations: Please check carefully for hallucinated references, which pose a serious concern to scientific reliability. Anonymity violations. As of January 2024, non-anonymous pre-prints are permitted for ARR, but submissions should still be properly anonymized (e.g., not containing explicit references to the authors’ prior work, acknowledgements, links to non-anonymous repositories or services like Dropbox that may track who opened the link). Style guides or length violations: the paper should be desk-rejected if it does not follow the style guides or goes over the page limit (4 pages for short, 8 for long papers, excluding the ethical considerations and limitations).

Since such data evolve rapidly based on events in the real world, as- suming a static language model becomes unrealistic. In general, more data is seen as better, but treating all past data equally runs the risk of distracting a model with irrelevant evidence. On the other hand, cau- tiously using only the most recent data risks overﬁt- ting to short-term trends and missing important time- insensitive effects (Blei and Lafferty, 2006; Wang et al., 2008). Therefore, in this paper, we take steps toward methods for capturing long-range temporal dynamics in language use. Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Why is peer review so inconsistent?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

Section: Q: Why is peer review so inconsistent?
Codes: none

Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.
